questions.text: A claim of $45,000 appears on a Bronze plan that normally caps claims at $10,000. This is an example of which outlier type?
options: Global outlier — extreme relative to all claims
Contextual outlier — extreme only within the Bronze plan context
Collective outlier — a group that is anomalous together
questions.explanation: A contextual outlier is extreme only within a specific context. $45,000 may not be unusual for Platinum plan claims, but it is extreme for Bronze, where coverage limits are much lower.

questions.text: The IQR rule flags a value as an outlier when it is:
options: More than 2 standard deviations from the mean
Below Q1 − 1.5 × IQR or above Q3 + 1.5 × IQR
More than 3 standard deviations from the mean
questions.explanation: The IQR rule uses Q1 − 1.5 × IQR as the lower fence and Q3 + 1.5 × IQR as the upper fence. Values beyond these fences are flagged. This is the standard box plot whisker rule.

questions.text: For fraud detection, outliers in claim_amount should always be removed to improve model accuracy.
questions.explanation: Fraudulent claims ARE the outliers — their unusual values are precisely what makes them detectable. Removing them would destroy the signal you are trying to model. For fraud, outliers should be flagged and retained, not removed.

questions.text: Winsorisation caps a variable to the [1st, 99th] percentile range. This is preferred over removal when:
options: The extreme values are clear data-entry errors
The extreme values are genuine but high-leverage, and you want to retain the record
You want to increase the variance of the variable
questions.explanation: Winsorisation retains the record but reduces the influence of extreme values. It is appropriate when the values are genuine (not errors) but would otherwise dominate distance calculations or regression coefficients.

questions.text: Why does log1p() produce a more symmetric distribution for claim_amount?
options: It removes all zeros from the data
It compresses large values more than small values, pulling the right tail in
It normalises the variable to mean 0 and SD 1
It converts the variable to ranks
questions.explanation: The logarithm compresses large values (the long right tail) more than small values. This makes the distribution more symmetric, which benefits algorithms that assume normality or compute Euclidean distances. log1p avoids undefined log(0) for zero-claim records.
